case.title: Chiller-plant electricity up 15% with flat production
case.setting: Velmora Plastics' Østrand site extrudes plastic profiles and moulds small components. A central plant of three 1,400 kW water-cooled centrifugal chillers (CH-1 to CH-3), two cooling towers and variable-speed secondary pumps supplies 7 °C process chilled water to the extrusion lines and other process users. The chiller plant's electricity (chillers, pumps, tower fans) is submetered at MCC-4. The site energy coordinator has escalated a sustained year-on-year rise in chiller-plant electricity that nobody on site can account for.
case.presentingRequest: The site director asks: why has chiller-plant electricity risen about 15% year on year when production is flat, and should she approve the chiller service vendor's €38,400 condenser cleaning now? She wants a recommendation this week.

initialEvidence.source: Energy summary prepared by the site energy coordinator, 3 Nov 2026
initialEvidence.text: Chiller plant (MCC-4 submeter: chillers, pumps, tower fans), Apr–Oct: 2025 1,412 MWh; 2026 1,628 MWh (+15.3%). Change vs same month of prior year: Jan +1%, Feb 0%, Mar +2%, Apr +4%, May +9%, Jun +14%, Jul +17%, Aug +18%, Sep +19%, Oct +20%. Site utility revenue meter, Apr–Oct: 3,520 → 3,738 MWh (+218 MWh). Site total minus MCC-4: 2,108 → 2,110 MWh. Weather, Tarnby airfield station: cooling degree-days Apr–Oct 2% lower in 2026 than 2025; mean daily wet-bulb 0.3 K lower. Extra chiller-plant cost for the period at current tariff ≈ €41,000.

initialEvidence.source: BMS 'Plant Efficiency' dashboard export, pulled 4 Nov 2026
initialEvidence.text: Plant efficiency = MCC-4 kWe ÷ kW of cooling delivered. Apr–Oct 2025 average 0.182 (monthly values 0.180–0.184). Apr–Oct 2026 average 0.209 (+15%). Monthly 2026: Apr 0.190, May 0.199, Jun 0.208, Jul 0.214, Aug 0.215, Sep 0.217, Oct 0.219. Cooling delivered, period average: 2025 1,510 kW; 2026 1,517 kW (+0.5%). Dashboard footnote: 'Cooling delivered = chilled-water header flow (FT-201) × (return temperature TT-202 − supply temperature TT-201) × fluid constant. Values shown as recorded.'

initialEvidence.source: Kestrel Cooling Services field service report, visit of 18 Sep 2026
initialEvidence.text: Visit to CH-1 at customer request. Readings at 92% load: leaving condenser water 29.4 °C, condensing temperature 31.3 °C, approach 1.9 K. The 2019 start-up sheet records an approach of 1.1 K; load at start-up is not recorded on our copy. Approach normally rises with load, but in our experience a 0.8 K increase points to tube fouling, likely following the change of water-treatment contractor in January. Tubes last brushed February 2025. CH-2 and CH-3 not measured this visit. Recommendation: mechanical brushing of all three condensers, €38,400, plus enrolment in our Performance Assurance contract (€14,200/yr) to prevent recurrence.

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, Tomas Reiner, production manager, 5 Nov 2026
initialEvidence.text: Shipped tonnage Apr–Oct is within 1% of last year and the product mix hasn't moved. We haven't added anything to the chilled-water loop. The moulding cell moved from Building C to the new Building F between April and June, but that was like-for-like, same presses, and Building F was designed with its own cooling. Please don't touch the water temperature: extrusion and the moulds need 7 °C supply. When it drifted to 8.5 °C for a week in 2024 we had a scrap spike on lines 2 and 3 and missed two customer deliveries.

initialEvidence.source: BMS change log excerpt and trend summary, Jan–Oct 2026
initialEvidence.text: 14 Mar 2026 09:12: SP-CHW (chilled-water supply setpoint) 7.0 → 6.0 °C, user 'ctrl-contractor', ticket 2231, comment 'trial for extrusion line 3 cooling'. 17 Mar 2026 15:40: SP-CHW 6.0 → 7.0 °C, same ticket, comment 'trial ended, no benefit'. No further SP-CHW changes to 31 Oct. Trend summary, supply temperature TT-201, monthly mean Apr–Oct: 2025 7.0 °C; 2026 7.1 °C. Chiller staging parameters: no changes logged since 2023.

initialEvidence.source: Email from plant shift lead to energy coordinator, 30 Oct 2026
initialEvidence.text: From about June we've had all three chillers on most afternoons. Last summer two usually carried it into the evening and CH-3 only came on in heat spells. Nothing is alarming. Header water has been in spec apart from a few late afternoons when line 3 grumbled about warm water. Honestly it feels like the machines are working harder for the same job; the dashboard says the same thing.

catalogue.title: Utility revenue-meter invoices and half-hourly interval data, Jan–Oct 2025 and 2026
catalogue.source: Northmere Energy invoices and data portal export
catalogue.text: Invoiced consumption Apr–Oct: 2025 3,519.6 MWh; 2026 3,737.9 MWh. Half-hourly data reconciles to the site's own summary within 0.2%. The increase is concentrated in 07:00–19:00 half-hours; night-time consumption is up about 4%. Meter serial and CT ratio unchanged since 2021. Supplier's annual meter accuracy test passed, March 2026.

catalogue.title: Tarnby airfield weather station daily dry-bulb and wet-bulb summaries, Apr–Oct 2025 and 2026
catalogue.text: Apr–Oct mean dry-bulb: 2025 15.8 °C, 2026 15.5 °C. Mean daily maximum wet-bulb: 2025 15.9 °C, 2026 15.6 °C. Hours with wet-bulb above 20 °C: 2025 212, 2026 188. Station is 14 km from site at similar elevation. Data-quality flags clear for both periods; no gaps longer than 3 hours.

catalogue.title: Cooling-water treatment contractor service visit sheets, Jan–Oct 2026
catalogue.text: Contract started 6 Jan 2026. Target cycles of concentration raised from 4.0 (previous contractor) to 5.0 to reduce make-up water. Conductivity within control band every month except 9–23 March (blowdown valve stuck, repaired 23 March). Inhibitor residual in range on 9 of 10 visits. Corrosion coupon rates acceptable. Calculated scaling index 'slightly positive, monitor' in July and August, neutral otherwise. Note on every sheet: 'Cannot comment on condenser tube surfaces without a waterbox being opened.'

catalogue.title: Chiller controller alarm and event logs, CH-1 to CH-3, Apr–Oct 2025 and 2026
catalogue.text: Events Apr–Oct: 2025 38, 2026 41. No high-condenser-pressure warnings or trips on any unit in either year. No surge events. CH-3: oil heater fault 11 Jul 2026, cleared after contactor replacement. CH-1: two 'low evaporator flow' warnings on 2 Aug 2026 during a secondary pump changeover, each cleared within 90 seconds. Remaining events are routine start/stop and sensor-check messages.

catalogue.title: Chiller run-hours and starts by unit, Apr–Oct 2025 and 2026
catalogue.text: Run-hours Apr–Oct, 2025 / 2026: CH-1 4,410 / 4,520; CH-2 4,180 / 4,390; CH-3 1,020 / 2,240. Starts: CH-3 96 / 171. Staging rule: add a chiller when running units exceed 90% of rated load (by motor current) for 15 minutes; rule unchanged since 2023. Average running-unit load at 2026 staging events: 91%.

catalogue.title: Calibration certificates and work-order history for chilled-water header flowmeter FT-201, 2022–2026
catalogue.source: CMMS records and controls contractor job sheets
catalogue.text: Last verified calibration of FT-201: June 2022. WO-5512, opened 14 Nov 2025: 'FT-201 reading drifts, jumps about ±15% intermittently.' Deferred. 2 Apr 2026: FT-201 converter failed after a power dip; replaced with a different-model converter by the controls contractor. Job sheet: 'Sensor calibration factor for existing flow tube not on file; default factor entered from datasheet. No wet verification performed; no reference meter available.' WO-5512 closed 3 Apr 2026 as 'converter replaced'. Note from controls engineer: secondary pumps are variable-speed on differential pressure, so header flow varies with demand and cannot be inferred from pump status.

catalogue.title: Condenser maintenance history, CH-1 to CH-3, 2019–2026
catalogue.text: Condensers brushed Feb 2023 and Feb 2025 under a 24-month contract interval; next brushing due Feb 2027. Eddy-current tube test Feb 2023: no tubes plugged, wall loss under 10% on all units. Feb 2025 brushing record: 'light soft deposit, removed.' No condenser waterbox opened since Feb 2025. CH-2 annual service outage booked 8–10 Dec 2026; planner notes a waterbox could be opened for a visual check within that window.

catalogue.title: ERP production summary by line and product family, Apr–Oct 2025 and 2026
catalogue.source: ERP report run by production planning
catalogue.text: Extrusion output: 2025 18,240 t; 2026 18,390 t. Moulded parts: 2025 4.11 million pieces; 2026 4.08 million. Product families unchanged; top-10 SKUs 71% of volume in 2025, 72% in 2026. Extrusion line run-hours: 2025 13,980 h; 2026 14,050 h. Moulding press count unchanged at 18.

catalogue.title: Cooling-tower BMS trends: condenser-water temperature, tower approach and fan speed, Apr–Oct 2025 and 2026
catalogue.source: BMS trend export and tower inspection sheet
catalogue.text: Monthly means Apr–Oct, 2025 / 2026: condenser-water supply temperature 24.8 / 24.9 °C; tower approach to ambient wet-bulb 4.1 / 4.6 K; tower fan VFD average speed 55% / 62%. Condenser-water flow is not metered. Tower fill inspected May 2026: 'clean, minor algae on distribution deck, cleaned.'

catalogue.title: Controls contractor ticket list and BMS parameter audit, chilled-water plant, Jan–Oct 2026
catalogue.source: Controls contractor service portal and audit report
catalogue.text: Tickets: #2231 supply setpoint trial 14–17 Mar (closed, setpoint restored); #2307 graphics update, May; #2312 alarm text corrections, June; #2355 add tower fan speed to dashboard, Aug. Parameter audit 20 Oct 2026: SP-CHW 7.0 °C; chiller staging rule, secondary pump differential-pressure setpoint (1.2 bar) and tower fan logic all match the 2023 baseline file.

catalogue.title: Facilities capital-project file CP-24-07, Building F mould-shop relocation, 2024–2026
catalogue.text: Design basis (2024): tool-cooling trim for Building F via dedicated 450 kW air-cooled chiller AC-F1. Change note CN-14, 12 Mar 2026: AC-F1 delivery slipped; interim arrangement approved by facilities manager: plate heat exchanger HX-F1 tied into the central chilled-water header, maximum transfer 400 kW, control valve modulated by the mould temperature units. Presses relocated in three phases: 6 on 8 Apr, 6 on 13 May, 6 on 10 Jun. HX-F1 commissioning sheet: 'valve stroked, flow observed.' No heat meter; valve position not trended; as-built drawings not yet issued. Production manager not on CN-14 distribution. AC-F1 now expected January 2027.

catalogue.title: Energy consultant desk review of chiller-plant performance, August 2026
catalogue.text: Desk review from BMS exports only; no site visit. 'Plant kWe/kWr has risen from 0.18 to 0.21 while delivered cooling is flat, a classic efficiency-degradation signature. Likely condenser fouling or refrigerant undercharge. Restoring design efficiency would save an estimated €60–70k per year.' Data sources listed: BMS Plant Efficiency dashboard; MCC-4 submeter. Instrument validation: 'not in scope.'

catalogue.title: Site electrical submeter breakdown for non-chiller loads, Apr–Oct 2025 and 2026
catalogue.text: Apr–Oct, 2025 → 2026 (MWh): extrusion 1,184 → 1,191; moulding (Building C in 2025; Buildings C and F in 2026) 402 → 405; compressed air 286 → 281; lighting and HVAC 172 → 169; other 64 → 64. Total 2,108 → 2,110. Building F office HVAC is on the lighting and HVAC meter.

catalogue.title: Statutory refrigerant leak-check log, CH-1 to CH-3, 2021–2026
catalogue.text: Leak checks March and September each year by certified technician (Kestrel Cooling Services). 2026 checks: no leaks detected on any unit. Recorded charge 410 kg per unit; no refrigerant added to any unit since 2021. Electronic detector calibration certificate attached for each visit.

catalogue.title: Plant operator shift logbook excerpts, June–August 2026
catalogue.text: '14 Jun: 3 chillers on from 13:20, header 7.2 °C.' '2 Jul: line 3 reports warm water 15:00–17:00, header read 7.6 °C, CH-1 and CH-2 at 97%.' '29 Jul: all three on, CH-1 at 96%.' '11 Jul: CH-3 tripped, oil heater, reset after contactor swap.' '19 Aug: quiet shift, two on until 12:40.' No entries mention setpoint changes.

hypotheses.text: The growth in chiller-plant electricity is explained by a decline in chiller efficiency (more electricity used per unit of cooling delivered).
The growth in chiller-plant electricity is explained by an increase in the cooling load the plant serves.
The reported growth is a metering artifact; actual chiller-plant electricity consumption has not risen.
Warmer or more humid weather in 2026 explains the growth in chiller-plant electricity.
A lowered chilled-water supply temperature setpoint has increased chiller work and explains the growth.

edges.from: Additional process heat load connected to the chilled-water loop
Change of water-treatment contractor in January 2026

actions.text: Before committing to maintenance or capital work, run a two-to-three-week measurement campaign: verify chilled-water header flow with an independently calibrated temporary meter, add temporary flow and temperature logging on every branch and connection drawing from the loop, and log per-chiller power.
Approve the vendor's €38,400 brushing of all three condensers now as the corrective action for the energy growth.
Raise the chilled-water supply setpoint from 7 °C to 9 °C plant-wide to cut chiller electricity while the cause is investigated.
Open one condenser waterbox for a visual tube inspection at the next scheduled single-chiller service outage.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: The chiller-plant electricity growth is real. The utility revenue meter shows a matching site increase, non-chiller loads are flat, the weather was milder and the March setpoint trial was reversed within three days. What the evidence cannot settle is whether the plant became less efficient or started serving more load. The dashboard's 15% efficiency loss is built on header flowmeter FT-201. That meter had an open drift work order before the 2025–26 comparison, was last verified in 2022, and its converter was replaced on 2 April 2026 with a default calibration factor and no wet check. Delivered cooling is therefore unknown in both years, and the apparent 'flat load, rising kWe/kWr' signature cannot be trusted. Separately, the Building F project quietly tied a heat exchanger of up to 400 kW into the central loop in April, because the dedicated air-cooled chiller was delayed. The production manager did not know this. Mould presses moved onto it in three phases from April to June, at the same time as the growth ramped. Nobody knows how much heat it actually carries: there is no heat meter or valve trend, and the as-built drawings are not issued. The vendor's fouling claim rests on a single CH-1 approach reading that is not matched for load, from an interested party. No catalogue item separates efficiency loss from load growth. The right move is a short, independently verified measurement campaign before spending on cleaning or capital work.

answers.rationale: The initial file seems to support H1. The dashboard shows kWe/kWr up 15% with flat delivered cooling, and the vendor and shift lead agree. C6 shows that delivered cooling comes from FT-201. That meter drifted ±15% before the baseline year, was last verified in 2022, and was re-converted in April 2026 with a default factor and no verification, so the efficiency metric is unreliable in both periods. The remaining support is one CH-1 approach reading from an interested vendor, compared with a start-up value at unknown load, which the vendor admits rises with load. Nothing contradicts efficiency loss either: the waterboxes have not been opened (C7, C3), and the absence of charge loss (C14) rules out only one mechanism. The claim is live but unestablished.

From the initial file, H2 looks contradicted: the production manager says nothing was added to the loop, and the dashboard shows flat cooling. C11 shows the manager is wrong. HX-F1, up to 400 kW, was tied into the central header in April, and presses moved onto it in phases that line up with the April–June ramp. The extra plant power is about 42 kWe on average. At roughly 0.18–0.19 kWe/kW that would need about 220 kW of transfer, which is within HX-F1's capacity but not shown, because there is no heat meter or valve trend. Flat production (C8, C13) does not rule out new chilled-water heat, because the tool cooling moved from the Building C tower to the central loop. Since the size of the added load is unknown, H2 is live but not established as the explanation.

The utility revenue meter rose by 218 MWh, the same as the MCC-4 increase, while site-minus-MCC-4 stayed flat at 2,108 → 2,110 MWh (E1). C1 adds an unchanged meter and a passed accuracy test. The FT-201 problem in C6 affects the cooling-delivered figure, not electricity, so an analyst who reads C6 and concludes that 'the growth is a meter problem' is mistaken.
Cooling degree-days were 2% lower and mean wet-bulb 0.3 K lower in 2026 (E1). C2 confirms this, with fewer high wet-bulb hours. Milder weather cannot explain a 15–20% rise.

The setpoint was lowered on 14 March and restored on 17 March, and no further changes were made. The supply temperature averaged 7.1 °C in Apr–Oct 2026 against 7.0 °C in 2025 (E5). The growth runs from April to October, when the setpoint was at its normal value. C10's audit confirms this.

The only measure of a decline in efficiency is the FT-201-based dashboard, which C6 invalidates. The consultant's memo (C12) simply repeats it. The vendor's approach reading measures condenser approach, not efficiency, and is not load-matched. Because the evidence does not show that the 'from' condition occurred at all, it cannot show it co-occurring with the growth. 'Causal', the initial-file reading, is not justified.

C11 documents an added process heat connection, and its phased loading (Apr, May, Jun) matches the ramp in E1, so the two co-occur and covary. It is not causal: the commissioning record shows only 'flow observed', the valve position and heat transfer were never measured, and the main rival (efficiency decline, possibly from fouling that builds up over the same months) has not been ruled out. Nothing counts against the link, so 'contradicted' is wrong. The manager's denial (E4) is refuted by C11.

The setpoint change lasted 14–17 March and was reversed. The supply temperature during the growth period matched the prior year (E5). Growth was +2% in March and only rose from April onward (E1). The link fails on timing and mechanism.

The treatment contractor change is documented, but a decline in efficiency is not established (C6 invalidates the metric), and no condenser surface has been seen since February 2025 (C7). C3 is ambiguous: one stuck blowdown valve and a slightly positive scaling index, with no inspection. The evidence cannot even show the two co-occurring.

Both leading explanations remain live because cooling delivered and branch loads are not measured reliably. Verified header flow, branch heat logging (which would capture HX-F1) and per-chiller power directly separate efficiency loss from load growth. The campaign is cheap and quick, and it does not disturb production.

If condenser fouling were confirmed, brushing would clearly help. It is not confirmed: the efficiency metric is invalid (C6) and the vendor's evidence is one reading that is not load-matched. If load growth is the explanation, brushing is money spent about three months ahead of the February 2027 contract interval (C7), with no lasting damage. Committing to it now as the corrective action is not justified.

The process needs 7 °C supply. At 8.5 °C in 2024 the site had scrap spikes and missed deliveries (E4). Raising the setpoint to 9 °C damages production whether the growth comes from efficiency loss or load growth. It would also distort the baseline that any measurement campaign depends on.

Looking at one condenser during an outage that is already planned is cheap and reasonable. It gathers evidence and commits to nothing. But it covers only one of three chillers and only one mechanism of efficiency loss, and it cannot measure or rule out load growth, so it is not among the best next actions compared with A1.

Any substantive step needs to know which explanation is true: condenser cleaning or a service contract if efficiency has declined, or bringing forward AC-F1 or rebalancing HX-F1 if load has grown. No item in the catalogue separates the two. The evidence is therefore insufficient to commit, and the only justified next step is to gather evidence.

truth.authoringNotes: Initial-file trap: the dashboard (E2), the vendor (E3) and the shift lead (E6) together point to efficiency loss, while the production manager (E4) and the dashboard's flat cooling appear to rule out load growth. A reader of the initial file alone will probably mark H1 supported, H2 contradicted, R1 causal, A2 preferred or acceptable, and SUFF sufficient. C6 alone removes the instrument behind the efficiency claim (H1 and R1 become unknown). C11 alone reveals the undisclosed HX-F1 tie-in (H2 becomes unknown, R2 association-only). Neither file appears anywhere else in the catalogue. C11 does not record where the tie-in sits relative to FT-201, so readers cannot use the flat dashboard cooling to infer HX-F1's load. No item gives chilled-water ΔT, refrigerant pressures, condenser-water flow or a heat meter, so readers cannot rebuild either the load or the lift. Confirmatory distractors: C1, C2, C10, C13, C14. Ambiguous distractors that look decisive but are not: C3 (treatment), C5 (run-hours), C9 (tower fan speed rises with both more load and more compressor work) and C12 (consultant repeats the dashboard). Monthly growth keeps rising into October; this fits progressive fouling, and it also fits a constant added load on a falling seasonal base, so the pattern does not separate the two. Arithmetic check: +216 MWh over 5,136 h ≈ 42 kWe ≈ 220–230 kW of cooling at 0.18–0.19 kWe/kW, which is within HX-F1's 400 kW maximum but not demonstrated. Reviewer check: H3 is a deliberate trap for readers who conflate the FT-201 cooling-meter fault with electricity metering.
